item.title: Sep 24 — 5 papers
item.description:
A relevance filter for collective perception messages has each vehicle send only the detected objects that matter for safety, and send them less often when nothing critical is happening; the authors report roughly the safety of 10 Hz full broadcasting at about a fifteenth of the bandwidth. The rest of the papers: an exact convergence test for distributed observers over switching networks when the system matrix commutes with the coupling matrices, which also covers unstable plants like vehicle platoons; a finite-sample bound for decentralized team learning with only private observations and delayed shared information; multi-robot exploration with probabilistic peer intent and multi-hop plan relay, where neither addition wins everywhere; and a result showing that networks with identical spectra can get opposite results from communicating.

  1. Frugal Collective Perception: Context-Aware Adaptive Reporting for Safety-Critical C-ITS — Romain Tessier et al.
    This is a relevance filter for collective perception messages. Each vehicle sends only the detected objects that matter for safety, and sends them less often when nothing critical is happening. The authors report roughly the safety of 10 hertz full broadcasting for about a fifteenth of the bandwidth.
  2. On stability of a distributed observer over switching networks: The case of commutative coupling — Sunghyun Koo, Jin Gyu Lee, Hyungbo Shim
    Koo, Lee and Shim show that if the system matrix commutes with the observer's coupling matrices, you get an exact necessary and sufficient test for when a distributed observer converges over a switching network, and that test also covers unstable plants such as a vehicle platoon.
  3. A Decentralized Partially Observable Team Decision Methodology with Delayed Information Sharing — Xiaoxing Ren, Thomas Parisini, Andreas A. Malikopoulos
    A theory paper showing that each member of a cooperative team can learn its own piece of a near-optimal team policy using only its private observations and team information that arrives with a delay, with no central coordinator and no known model, and with a finite-sample bound on how much data this takes.
  4. Decentralized Multi-Robot Exploration with Probabilistic Peer Intent and Multi-hop Plan Propagation — Saurbh Singh Jamwal, Nived Chebrolu, Shivaram Kalyanakrishnan
    The authors take an existing decentralized tree-search planner for multi-robot exploration and add two things. Shared peer waypoints get smeared into a probability map of where teammates will go, and plans get relayed over multiple hops. Neither addition wins everywhere.
  5. When Does Communication Help? Beyond Spectral Descriptions of Collective Intelligence — Xuening Wu
    Two networks of agents can share identical eigenvalue and singular-value spectra and still get opposite results from communicating, so predicting whether talking helps means using a task-aware local-response model, not a spectral summary.

item.title: Sep 23 — 5 papers
item.description:
Network-flow constraints that keep a multi-vehicle MILP planner's communication graph connected scale better for plain connectivity but give no average speedup for k-hop connectivity. Nash and Stackelberg intersection controllers, moved from MATLAB onto Quanser QCar 2 scale cars, start to suffer from sensing and state-estimation noise, and robots that share frozen perception embeddings instead of positions learn from reward alone to detect an occluded hazard in 99.7% of episodes. Also covered: a VCG-style auction where drone operators bid for slots in a shared safe corridor and gain nothing by misreporting their costs, and a scenario-based MPC that writes driving rules in signal temporal logic and, when the rules can't all be met, relaxes them with a Pareto tradeoff across several agents rather than protecting only the ego vehicle.

  1. Mixed-integer flow formulations for motion planning and decision-making of networked multi-agent systems — Angelo Caregnato-Neto et al.
    The authors replace subtour-elimination constraints with network-flow constraints to keep a multi-vehicle MILP planner's communication graph connected, and find this scales better for plain connectivity but gives no average speedup for k-hop connectivity.
  2. Hardware-in-the-Loop Evaluation of Game-Theoretic Autonomous Driving — Aakanksha Kataria, Huiwen Yan, Mushuang Liu
    The authors take existing Nash and Stackelberg intersection-crossing controllers, run them on Quanser QCar 2 scale cars through a staged pipeline from MATLAB to a simulator to physical hardware, and find that sensing and state-estimation noise matter once the controllers leave simulation.
  3. Latent Telepathy: Multi-Robot Communication with Self-Supervised Perceptual Latents — Howard Wang, Han Zheng, Cathy Wu
    Instead of sending each other positions or planned trajectories, robots broadcast the frozen perception embedding they already compute. A teammate learns from reward alone to read an occluded hazard out of it, and it does so in 99.7 percent of episodes.
  4. Paying for Space: Incentive-Aware Motion Planning for Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance — Debajyoti Chakrabarti, Anushri Dixit
    They let drone operators bid for slots in a shared safe corridor, and use a VCG-style payment so that lying about your own costs never gets you a better trajectory.
  5. Scenario MPC with STL Specifications and Pareto-Based Feasibility Repair — Tianhao Wu, Yiwei Lyu
    An MPC controller that encodes driving rules in signal temporal logic, handles uncertain surrounding vehicles by sampling scenarios, and when the rules become impossible to satisfy, relaxes them by picking a Pareto tradeoff across several agents' objectives instead of only protecting the ego vehicle.

item.title: Sep 22 — 2 papers
item.description:
Bearing-only leader-follower formation control normally inherits whatever exponential convergence rate the formation's excitation happens to supply; the first paper replaces the fixed gain with a gain matrix adapted to the bearings each follower actually measures, making the rate something you prescribe rather than observe. The second takes independent LQG plants sharing a single channel with a hard per-step cap on transmitters and shows the controllers still separate agent by agent, leaving scheduling as the only coupled piece — posed as a mixed integer program and then approximated by a cheap auction.

  1. Leader-Follower Formation Control with Prescribed Convergence Rates under Bearing Persistence of Excitation — Tarek Bouazza et al.
    They replace the fixed gain in bearing-only leader-follower formation control with a gain matrix that adapts to the bearings each follower actually sees, so you can dial in the exponential convergence rate instead of inheriting whatever rate the formation's excitation happens to give you.
  2. Multi-Agent Event-Triggered LQG Control under Shared Communication Constraints — Zahra Hashemi, Dipankar Maity
    When a group of independent LQG plants share one channel with a hard cap on how many can transmit per step, the controllers still decouple agent by agent, and the only hard part left is deciding who gets to speak, which they solve with a mixed integer program and then approximate with a cheap auction.

The second takes independent LQG plants sharing a single channel with a hard per-step cap on transmitters and shows the controllers still separate agent by agent, leaving scheduling as the only coupled piece — posed as a mixed integer program and then approximated by a cheap auction.

item.title: Sep 19 — 5 papers
item.description:
Five papers on keeping multi-agent systems coordinated when the assumptions underneath them shift: per-robot position boxes that turn "the communication graph stays connected" into a local constraint each robot can satisfy alone, crowd navigation that carries a belief about each individual pedestrian's responsiveness forward between replans, and a learned similarity metric over opponent driving styles that separates an aggressive blocker from a passive line-holder within a few laps and feeds its predicted uncertainty into overtake decisions on a 1/10-scale racecar. Two networking papers work the other direction, from simulator fidelity to attack surface — one fits a closed-form packet-loss formula to 10.5M labeled ns-3 5G-LENA sidelink receptions so Veins/SUMO users get realistic Mode-2 delivery rates without implementing Mode-2, the other shows that spoofing a rain sensor cuts a platoon's usable mmWave link range in half without ever touching the radio channel.

  1. Distributed Model Predictive Control with Connectivity-based Contracts — Jorit Geurts et al.
    Every robot in the team gets handed a box it must keep its predicted positions inside, and the boxes are constructed so that if everyone respects their own box, the communication graph cannot break.
  2. TRACER: Adaptive Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Joint Human-Response Prediction and Interaction-Aware Replanning — Lan Hu et al.
    Robots moving through crowds pick team trajectories by predicting how each nearby human will react, then remember what that specific human actually did and carry that belief forward into the next replan.
  3. NS3Learn: Transferring 5G NR Mode-2 Reception Realism from ns-3 to the Veins/SUMO Stack for Connected-Vehicle Safety Assessment — Rasheed Bello et al.
    They ran full ns-3 5G-LENA sidelink simulations, labeled ten and a half million reception outcomes, and fit a closed-form packet-loss formula that lets a Veins and SUMO user get realistic Mode-2 delivery rates without ever implementing the Mode-2 protocol.
  4. Kernel-Based Metrics Learning for Uncertain Opponent Vehicle Trajectory Prediction in Autonomous Racing — Hojin Lee et al.
    They learn a similarity metric over opponent driving styles so a Gaussian-process-style predictor can tell an aggressive blocker from a passive line-holder after a few laps of watching, and then use the predicted uncertainty to pick safe overtakes on a one-tenth scale racecar.
  5. Weather Data Spoofing Attacks on Rain-Adaptive Millimeter-Wave Frequency Selection in V2X Communication Networks — Rasheed Bello et al.
    If you let a car pick its mmWave band from the rain it thinks is falling, you can spoof the rain sensor and quietly cut a platoon's usable link range in half without ever touching the radio channel.

item.title: Sep 18 — 5 papers
item.description:
Three papers on coordination when the radio link is unreliable: a MARL method that regularizes learned messages to reduce uncertainty about future states and then stress-tests them under bandwidth caps and packet loss, a 500-instance head-to-head of six decentralized task allocators that finds no single winner across route quality, message volume, and compute time, and an exploration planner that solves a small orienteering problem at scheduled check-ins to decide whether driving back into radio range is worth the detour. Two applied control papers round it out: per-worker tuning of health-alert frequency for construction workers modelled as losing trust in an app that nags them, compared between a short-horizon controller and reinforcement learning, and a Unity lettuce-growth simulator that renders synthetic crop image time-series so vision-based greenhouse controllers can be trained without labelled plant photos.

  1. Robust and Efficient Communication for Multi-Agent Learning — Rafael Pina, Varuna De Silva, Corentin Artaud
    A MARL communication method that regularizes learned messages to reduce uncertainty about future states, and then stress-tests those messages under bandwidth limits and packet loss instead of assuming a perfect channel.
  2. Decentralized Multi-Robot Task Allocation Under Degraded Communication: A Benchmark of Performance, Reliability, and Computation — James Lott, Vahraz Honary
    They ran six decentralized task-allocation algorithms head to head over five hundred paired instances with lossy radios, and found no single winner — different allocators own different corners of the tradeoff space between route quality, message volume, and compute time.
  3. Personalized and Trust-Aware Health Recommendation Policies for a Construction Workplace — Atefeh Mollabagher et al.
    They build a control model of construction workers who lose trust in a health app that nags them, and then tune how often the app should fire an alert per worker using both a short-horizon controller and reinforcement learning.
  4. LettuceVisSim: A Simulator That Generates Lettuce Image Time-series for Vision-Based Reinforcement Learning — Ziye Zhu et al.
    A lettuce growth simulator that renders synthetic time-series crop images in Unity so you can train vision-based reinforcement learning controllers for greenhouses without collecting labelled plant photos.
  5. Communication-Constrained Multi-Robot Exploration With Adaptive Communication Windows — Ben Rossano, Jaein Lim, Jonathan P. How
    Robots exploring an unknown map decide, at scheduled check-in times, whether it is actually worth driving back to a spot where they can radio each other, by solving a small orienteering problem that credits the exploration they can do along the way.

Two applied control papers round it out: per-worker tuning of health-alert frequency for construction workers modelled as losing trust in an app that nags them, compared between a short-horizon controller and reinforcement learning, and a Unity lettuce-growth simulator that renders synthetic crop image time-series so vision-based greenhouse controllers can be trained without labelled plant photos.

item.title: Sep 17 — 2 papers
item.description:
CoAdapt puts an LLM in the runtime loop as a dispatcher that reads a text description of the scene and decides which robots contribute to LiDAR fusion and which fusion algorithm runs, cutting communication cost 38% on OPV2V. The second paper shows that optimizing a status-update link for freshness alone leaves bursty gaps between consecutive updates, and its controller over finite-state Markov channels accepts 8.3% worse average age in exchange for 37.3% fewer joint threshold violations.

  1. CoAdapt: An LLM-based Framework for Adaptive Collaborative Perception in IIoT Robotic Swarms — Houssam Hajj Hassan et al.
    They put an LLM in the loop as a runtime dispatcher that reads a text description of the scene and decides which robots get to contribute to the LiDAR fusion and which fusion algorithm runs, saving 38 percent of communication cost on OPV2V.
  2. Joint Freshness and Age-Dispersion Control over Finite-State Markov Wireless Channels — Aresh Dadlani et al.
    They show that if you only chase freshness on a status update link, you get bursty gaps between consecutive updates, and their controller trades 8.3 percent worse average age for 37.3 percent fewer joint threshold violations.

item.title: Sep 16 — 4 papers
item.description:
**Episode description:** > Two decentralized coordination methods: robots that learn a latent message code whose decoded output drives a flow-matching policy for short collision-free motion segments, and a cooperative vector field whose avoidance reaction zone is sized to the path curvature a car-like robot can actually achieve. Two infrastructure-side proposals: treating tunnel positioning as a roadside tracking problem with fiber-optic distributed acoustic sensing instead of dead reckoning from the last GNSS fix, and reassigning roadside units across SDN controllers under load, which lowered end-to-end delay and packet loss versus single- and fixed-controller setups in Mininet-WiFi emulation. Two notes on choices: I split it robot-side / infrastructure-side rather than one sentence per pair of papers, since that's the real fault line in the set. I also kept "in Mininet-WiFi emulation" attached to the SDVN result rather than dropping it for length — it's the one claim in the set with a measured number behind it, and the number is emulation-only. Note: file-read tools aren't available in this session, so I couldn't check `episodes/*.json` for the house description format (length cap, casing, whether descriptions usually lead with the topic). If those files have a convention, tell me and I'll match it.

  1. Learning Communication-Conditioned Generative Policies for Decentralized Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance — Prajwal Koirala, Mark Campbell
    Robots learn to talk to each other in a made-up latent language, and a flow-matching policy turns those messages into short bursts of collision-free motion without any central planner.
  2. Distributed Safe Cooperative Vector Field for Trajectory Curvature Constrained Multi-Robot Systems — Zhouru Xiao et al.
    They give a team of car-like robots a vector field that steers them along assigned paths and around each other, with the collision-avoidance reaction zone sized so the robot can actually make the turn it is being asked to make.
  3. Beyond Dead Reckoning: A Point of View on Camera--DAS--GNSS Continuity in Road Tunnels — Lyes Saad Saoud et al.
    A position paper arguing that tunnel positioning for automated vehicles should stop being dead reckoning from the last GNSS fix and instead become an infrastructure-side tracking problem, with fiber optic distributed acoustic sensing as the continuous motion sensor.
  4. Enhancing SDVN Performance via Policy-Driven Lightweight Control-Plane Resizing Strategies — Muhammad Zain Ul Abideen et al.
    They move roadside units between SDN controllers when one controller gets overloaded, and show in Mininet-WiFi emulation that this cuts end-to-end delay and packet loss versus running a single controller or a fixed set of controllers.

item.title: Sep 13 — 1 papers
item.description:
A Northeastern group argues that Open RAN's split of softwarized radios, an external controller, and pluggable apps generalizes beyond cellular, letting radar, GPS, and cellular tenants share antennas and compute rather than only dividing up frequency. Ray-traced simulation gives up to 12 dB of median SINR gain from that pooled infrastructure, though the case rests on simulation rather than a deployed multi-tenant testbed, and the paper leaves the cross-operator trust and scheduling latency questions to future work.

  1. From Open RAN to Open Spectrum: A Programmable, Intelligent Architecture for Multi-Service Spectrum Coexistence — Michele Polese et al.
    A team from Northeastern proposes extending Open RAN's softwarized, controller-plus-app model from cellular networks to spectrum sharing generally, so that radar, GPS, and cellular tenants pool not just frequencies but also antennas and compute, and they show in ray-traced simulation that sharing infrastructure buys up to twelve decibels of median SINR.

item.title: Sep 12 — 3 papers
item.description:
Two papers on estimation and control under a broken channel, one on shared-world simulation: a multi-sensor fusion estimator that still recovers state when data packets arrive with scrambled sender identities, modeling the mix-up as an unknown permutation to either average over or pick the most likely; and a predefined-time sliding-mode consensus protocol for second-order agents that freezes its internal convergence clock during each denial-of-service blackout and restarts it when links return, so the deadline guarantee survives jamming. CARLAverse puts a driving simulator, a bike simulator, and a pedestrian walking rig into one CARLA world simultaneously, with each participant's vehicle physics and force feedback computed on local hardware instead of across the network.

  1. Fusion Estimation in Multi-sensor Systems for Data Packets with Disrupted Identities — Haoyuan Xu, Yuzhe Li
    If your fusion center can't tell which sensor sent which measurement, this paper works out how to estimate anyway by treating the mix-up as an unknown permutation and either averaging over all of them or betting on the most likely one.
  2. Predefined-Time Leaderless Consensus Under Denial-of-Service Attacks — Lohitvel Gopikannan, Shashi Ranjan Kumar, Abhinav Sinha
    A sliding-mode consensus protocol for second-order agents that keeps a guaranteed convergence deadline even when the communication graph is jammed, by freezing its internal clock during each blackout and restarting it when links come back.
  3. CARLAverse: A Highly Modular, Distributed, and Multimodal Framework for Human-in-the-Loop Simulation — Patrick Rebling, Philipp Nenninger, Reiner Kriesten
    They wired a driving simulator, a bike simulator, and a pedestrian walking rig into one shared CARLA world, and the trick that makes it work is running each participant's own vehicle physics and force feedback locally instead of over the network.

CARLAverse puts a driving simulator, a bike simulator, and a pedestrian walking rig into one CARLA world simultaneously, with each participant's vehicle physics and force feedback computed on local hardware instead of across the network.

item.title: Sep 11 — 5 papers
item.description:
A vehicle-in-the-loop study shows that sharing planned intent rather than current status keeps a follower from crashing when its V2X link is hit with up to two seconds of denial-of-service delay, and a rolling-horizon, bounded-horizon Conflict Based Search over spline roadmaps routes differently-sized warehouse AGVs through narrow two-way corridors for up to eleven percent more throughput than the rule-based scheme a real factory would run. Three more papers round it out: a proof that single-state agents communicating over a directed network can hold a common moving safety corridor and reach consensus despite different asymmetric actuator saturation limits, an uncertainty-aware control barrier function layered on distributional reinforcement learning so the safety filter tightens only where the policy is unsure at unsignalized intersections, and a drift correction that snaps short odometry segments onto OpenStreetMap lane centerlines whether the odometry came from LiDAR or a camera.

  1. Mitigating Degradation Attacks in Cooperative Autonomous Driving via Intention Sharing: A Vehicle-in-the-Loop Study — Prakhar Gupta et al.
    They put a real drive-by-wire car in the loop, jammed its V2X link with up to two seconds of denial-of-service delay, and showed that sharing planned intent instead of current status stops the follower from crashing.
  2. A traffic management system for large and heterogeneous vehicles in narrow industrial environments — Alessandro Bonetti et al.
    They coordinate warehouse AGVs of different sizes through narrow two-way corridors using a rolling-horizon, bounded-horizon Conflict Based Search over spline roadmaps, and get up to eleven percent more throughput than the rule-based system a real factory would use today.
  3. Networked Admissibility-Preserving Control for Directed Safe Coordination — Abhinav Sinha, Lohitvel Gopikannan, Shashi Ranjan Kumar
    A control-theory paper proving that a group of single-state agents talking over a directed network can hold a common moving safety corridor and hit consensus even when each actuator has different asymmetric saturation limits.
  4. A Risk-Sensitive and Uncertainty-Aware Decision-Making and Control Framework for Safe and Robust Autonomous Driving — Zhuoren Li et al.
    They bolt an uncertainty-aware control barrier function onto distributional reinforcement learning so the safety filter tightens only when the policy itself is unsure, tested on unsignalized intersection crossings in simulation.
  5. Odometer-Agnostic Drift Correction Using OpenStreetMap Lane Geometry — Joaquin Caballero et al.
    They snap short chunks of odometry onto OpenStreetMap lane centerlines to kill long-term drift, and it works regardless of whether the odometry came from LiDAR or a camera.

Three more papers round it out: a proof that single-state agents communicating over a directed network can hold a common moving safety corridor and reach consensus despite different asymmetric actuator saturation limits, an uncertainty-aware control barrier function layered on distributional reinforcement learning so the safety filter tightens only where the policy is unsure at unsignalized intersections, and a drift correction that snaps short odometry segments onto OpenStreetMap lane centerlines whether the odometry came from LiDAR or a camera.

item.title: Sep 10 — 5 papers
item.description:
Two UCF UrbanTwin sim-to-real LiDAR reports push the same synthetic-only setup in opposite directions: one takes the V2X-Real roadside track by training four differently corrupted point cloud sets into separate DSVT expert branches and hand-wiring which branch votes on which class, while the LUMPI track winner concedes that the synthetic clouds looked convincing and the detector still barely worked. The rest is control and coordination — a string-stability result that drops the H-infinity test for a direct no-growing-eigenmodes condition and stabilizes mixed traffic with far fewer AVs than prior bounds demand, twenty cities of simulated delivery vans whose shared selfish charging policy reads broadcast station occupancy and cuts queue waits from roughly forty-five minutes to under two, and Hi-FLoop's nested eight-second/two-second/one-second traffic rollout that commits only the half-second slice actually executed to memory.

  1. Solution for UCF UrbanTwin V2X-Real Track: Sim-to-Real Urban LiDAR 3D Object Detection — Pu Luo et al.
    A contest report that wins a roadside LiDAR sim-to-real leaderboard by training four differently corrupted synthetic point cloud sets into separate DSVT expert branches, then hand-wiring which branch gets to vote on which object class.
  2. Stabilizing Traffic Flow Via Autonomous Vehicles: A Less Conservative Approach — MirSaleh Bahavarnia, Ahmad F. Taha
    They swap out the standard H-infinity string-stability test for a direct no-growing-eigenmodes condition, and show you can stabilize mixed traffic with far fewer autonomous vehicles than the literature claims you need.
  3. Emergent Charging Coordination in Electric Delivery Fleets — Javier Vales-Alonso, Juan J. Alcaraz
    Twenty cities of simulated delivery vans each run the same selfish charging policy, learned by neuroevolution or PPO, and just by reading broadcast station occupancy they stop piling onto the same charger, cutting queue waits from about forty-five minutes to under two.
  4. Solution for UCF UrbanTwin LUMPI Track: Sim-to-Real Urban LiDAR 3D Object Detection — Pu Luo et al.
    A five-page ECCV challenge report on winning a synthetic-only LiDAR detection track, where the honest headline is that the fake point clouds looked great and the detector barely worked.
  5. Hi-FLoop: Hierarchical State-Feedback Loops for Multi-Timescale World Modeling — Rx Fan, Zhan H
    It generates eight-second multi-agent traffic futures by splitting the rollout into nested time scales, an eight-second goal, a two-second preview, and a one-second control step, and it only lets the half-second slice that actually executed become memory for the next step.

item.title: Sep 9 — 3 papers
item.description:
Three papers that buy timeliness by deliberately computing less: an edge node that takes over sensor fusion and path prediction for connected vehicles but caps how many vehicles it fuses per cycle so the answer arrives before it goes stale; Wongpiromsarn's risk-aware rulebooks, which attach a risk measure and acceptable threshold to each prioritized traffic rule and solve the lexicographic problem with anytime branch-and-bound, returning a policy plus a certified suboptimality bound; and a JEPA-style world model that jointly predicts a teleoperated robot's trajectory and its radio channel, using both to decide when a camera frame can be skipped. Each one names a deadline and then discards information to meet it — unfused vehicles, an early-stopped search, a dropped frame — and none of the three establishes what the discarded information would have been worth.

  1. Scalable Edge-assisted Fusion and Path Prediction for Connected Autonomous Vehicles — Tyler Landle et al.
    They move the sensor fusion and trajectory prediction off the vehicles and onto a roadside edge node, then throttle how many vehicles get fused each cycle so the answer arrives before it goes stale.
  2. Risk-Aware Optimal Control with Rulebooks — Tichakorn Wongpiromsarn
    Wongpiromsarn takes rulebooks, the prioritized traffic-rule hierarchy from the autonomous driving literature, attaches a risk measure and an acceptable threshold to each rule, and solves the resulting lexicographic problem with an anytime branch-and-bound that hands you a policy plus a certified bound on how suboptimal it might be.
  3. Coupled Control and Wireless World Models for Resilient Remote Robotic Control — H. P. Madushanka, Sumudu Samarakoon, Mehdi Bennis
    They train a JEPA-style world model that predicts both where a wirelessly teleoperated robot is going and what the radio channel will do next, and use those joint predictions to decide when the robot can skip sending a camera frame.
item.itunes:summary: Three papers that buy timeliness by deliberately computing less: an edge node that takes over sensor fusion and path prediction for connected vehicles but caps how many vehicles it fuses per cycle so the answer arrives before it goes stale; Wongpiromsarn's risk-aware rulebooks, which attach a risk measure and acceptable threshold to each prioritized traffic rule and solve the lexicographic problem with anytime branch-and-bound, returning a policy plus a certified suboptimality bound; and a JEPA-style world model that jointly predicts a teleoperated robot's trajectory and its radio channel, using both to decide when a camera frame can be skipped. Each one names a deadline and then discards information to meet it — unfused vehicles, an early-stopped search, a dropped frame — and none of the three establishes what the discarded information would have been worth.

item.title: Sep 7 — 5 papers
item.description:
Today's briefing covers 5 new papers.

  1. Risk-Aware Optimal Control with Rulebooks — Tichakorn Wongpiromsarn
    It turns a priority-ordered rulebook of driving requirements into a lexicographic optimization over how much each rule's risk exceeds its allowed threshold, and solves it with an anytime branch-and-bound that hands you a policy plus a certified bound on how suboptimal it is.
  2. Open-Loop Stackelberg LQ Difference Games with Coupled-Affine Inequality Constraints: An Exact OCP--LCS/LCQP Reformulation — Shrestha Ghosh, Puduru Viswanadha Reddy
    They show that a leader-follower linear-quadratic game with hard inequality constraints coupling both players can be rewritten exactly as a single optimal control problem with complementarity conditions built in, which finally makes the equilibrium computable.
  3. Coupled Control and Wireless World Models for Resilient Remote Robotic Control — H. P. Madushanka, Sumudu Samarakoon, Mehdi Bennis
    They train a JEPA-style world model that predicts both a robot's future state and the wireless channel's future state from camera frames plus radio spectrograms, and use those joint predictions to decide when the robot can skip an uplink transmission.
  4. Human-Human & Human-Robot Interaction Transformer (H2INT) for Robot Navigation in Dense and Uncertain Crowds — Ao Shen et al.
    They train a robot to push through crowded corridors by keeping the pedestrians reactive during learning, and by letting each pedestrian be more or less willing to yield, which the robot has to figure out on the fly from how people are positioned relative to it.
  5. A Schema Bounded Language Model for Refining Robot Policies Without Destabilizing Local Learning — Chongwen Dong et al.
    Three simulated robots each run their own language model to write a navigation policy once per round, a bandit to pick how to revise it, and a Double DQN to actually steer, and the full stack reaches the goal in every trial with a median of 42 ticks.
